summary: Scoping call to agree success criteria and integration approach for a POC benchmark. Customer wants a mixed-mode harness that defaults to streaming for short prompts, falls back to non-streaming batched requests for heavy loads, and preserves end-to-end ordering and idempotency. Discussed telemetry hooks, error handling, KV/prefix caching semantics, and SLO targets. Agreed on next steps to exchange scripts and run a 48h baseline in Redwood sandbox.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-05-06 16:00 UTC
Duration: 46 min
Attendees: Maya Chen, Diego Alvarez, Nina Patel (Redwood) -- Priya Singh, Liam O'Connor, Jordan Park, Eve Morales (BrightStreet)

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Priya (BrightStreet): Priya here. Hi all.
[00:09] Liam (BrightStreet): Liam on for platform.
[00:11] Jordan (BrightStreet): Jordan SRE.
[00:13] Maya: Great. Diego, want to intro the tech goals?
[00:16] Diego (Redwood SE): Yeah, super quick. We want to map your load profile and agree on success criteria for the POC. From past calls the ask was mixed-mode harness: streaming for interactive flows but a reliable fallback to non-streaming batching for bulk scoring, also maintain ordering and idempotency.
[00:35] Priya: Correct. For our case we have interactive product help queries where latency matters — users expect near realtime — and also nightly batch embeddings where throughput and cost matter. We also need consistent outputs for A/B testing.
[00:52] Maya: Perfect. Can you give us target numbers? P95 latency target, token rates, concurrency?
[00:57] Priya: For interactive we want p95 < 350 ms on generation tail for the short-turn prompts (~50-80 tokens). For batch, it's more about throughput: we expect up to 4k seqs per minute during peak ingest windows.
[01:15] Liam: And our client calls have a steady-state of ~120 rps for embeddings during business hours, with spikes up to ~400 rps. We can shape that into streaming or batch.
[01:27] Diego: Okay, that helps. For streaming we usually recommend keeping message sizes small and using prefix caching when you have many similar prompts. Note prefix cache here refers to KV cache — sometimes speech-to-text transcriptions call it K-V cash — so forgive the slur.
[01:43] Priya: Haha, noted. Our main worry is fallback behavior: if streaming backend backs up, we can't drop user messages or reorder them unpredictably.
[01:52] Nina (Redwood): Right, so the harness should implement a short window buffer and then switch to batched call with the same session token to preserve ordering. Also idempotency keys per user request to dedupe on retry.
[02:07] Jordan: How do you handle partial streams? Say a generation begins streaming then backend fails mid-token?
[02:12] Diego: Two behaviors: one is deterministic restart which replays last known KV to pick up, second is to fail and surface a consistent error to the client. For POC we can prototype both and measure user-visible recovery time.
[02:24] [02:30] Priya: For benchmarks we need: latency distribution (p50/p90/p95/p99), token cost per million, success/failure rate, and a quality metric where we run 1k unit prompts and check semantic similarity to a golden set.
[02:45] Maya: Good list. Any compliance/security items? Jordan?
[02:50] Jordan: SOC2 compliance is baseline. For Private deployment we need KMS integration and audit logs, also VPC peering or private link. We'll share our security checklist.
[03:03] Diego: We'll also point telemetry hooks: request_id, customer_tenant, route, batch_id, token_count. That helps correlate with your APM.
[03:12] Liam: On network diagram, we have a NATed VPC with egress limits. If you require client-to-private endpoints we'll need an on-prem connector.
[03:22] Maya: Ok noted. Let's outline the POC success criteria — Diego?
[03:26] Diego: My suggested POC success criteria: 1) Streaming p95 latency <350ms for short prompts (50-80 tokens) under target concurrency. 2) Batch throughput >= target 4k sequences/min with 95% success. 3) Semantic drift <= 5% measured by our similarity eval on the 1k test set. 4) End-to-end error/recovery window <3s for streaming fallback. 5) Operational readiness: logs and telemetry in place and a reproducible harness adapter checked into your repo.
[03:58] Priya: That aligns. On cost we want an estimate: we have an internal target of <$25 per 1M tokens for batch scoring.
[04:08] Maya: We'll provide cost estimates for both hosted and dedicated tiers, plus quantized model variants if you want lower cost per token.
[04:15] [04:30] Eve (BrightStreet): Quick Q: Do you support model pinning and rollout policies during the POC? We might want to test a new quantized variant and roll back if quality drops.
[04:36] Diego: Yes, platform supports model pinning, canary, and automatic fallback to a baseline model. For the harness, we recommend a config flag that hits the canary endpoint and a circuit-breaker to fallback. We'll include that in the adapter.
[04:50] Priya: For the harness itself, we have custom client libraries in Go for our product — is there a preferred adapter language?
[04:57] Nina: We have adapters in Node/Python/Go. For Go we provide a small example that shows streaming event handling, backpressure, and batch fallthrough. We'll attach that.
[05:09] Liam: How do we validate tokenization parity across our stack and Redwood? Tokenizers sometimes differ and that affects token counting/cost.
[05:17] Diego: We can share tokenizer binaries or a deterministic tokenization service. For the POC, please send a small corpus and we'll run tokenization parity tests.
[05:26] [05:40] Priya: Regarding telemetry, we want the ability to slice by customer_id, prompt_template, and A/B cohort. Can Redwood ship those labels?
[05:48] Maya: Yes — we'll include those fields in the telemetry schema; we can map to your APM tags.
[05:53] Jordan: Network and security again — if we run the sandbox in your hosted environment, how long do logs persist? We need at least 90 days for debugging.
[06:01] Diego: Hosted sandbox defaults to 7 days, but for POC we can extend to 90 days as a temporary config. For private/on-prem we'll align with your retention.
[06:13] [06:30] Priya: Benchmark windows — we propose two parts: warmup + steady-state (48h baseline) and then a stress window (4 hours) that includes spikes up to 2x peak.
[06:41] Maya: That works. Redwood to run baseline with your real traffic trace if you share it. We'll run both streaming and batch scenarios and produce a combined report.
[06:52] Diego: On harness details, important items: backpressure signals (client side), idle stream tombstones to release KV cache, and connector-level idempotency keys. Also, telemetry should include batch ids so we can trace batched requests back to the stream.
[07:11] Priya: For idempotency keys, we want to reuse client-generated UUIDs. If a request is retried we must not double bill or double embed.
[07:20] Nina: We'll honor client idempotency headers and surface a retry-count metric. We'll also include opt-in dedupe window settings.
[07:28] [07:40] Liam: A nit — latency numbers are different between cold-start and warm workers. Do you have cold-start mitigation?
[07:45] Diego: Yes, pre-warmed pools and predictive scaling heuristics. For the POC we'll reserve a small pool to minimize cold starts during the baseline. We'll log cold-start events.
[07:56] Priya: Can we get a sample benchmark report schema? We want to map to our exec metrics.
[08:02] Maya: We'll attach a sample report — includes latency percentiles, error taxonomy, cost breakdown, and quality delta vs golden.
[08:12] [08:30] Jordan: Regarding encryption, does the sandbox support customer-managed keys?
[08:35] Diego: For hosted sandbox we can do envelope encryption; customer-managed keys for Private or dedicated plans. For POC evaluation we can do a limited KMS integration demo.
[08:46] Priya: Great. About quality checks: we want an automated regression alert if similarity drops >3% for the golden prompts. Can Redwood run that?
[08:54] Nina: Yes, Redwood Optimize can integrate evals and send regression alerts tied to the test set. We'll turn that on for the POC.
[09:02] [09:15] Maya: Let's talk about observability: what logs/metrics do you need in the first week?
[09:19] Priya: Request-id traces, p95/p99 latency by route, tokens consumed, failures by error code, and a sample of generation outputs for manual QA.
[09:28] Diego: We'll provide all that. We'll also add a sampling mechanism to capture full outputs for 0.1% of requests to avoid PII leakage.
[09:38] Priya: Good call. We also need to consider redaction for PII in the transcripts.
[09:43] Nina: We can apply redaction rules client-side or via our ingestion pipeline. We'll include examples.
[09:51] [10:10] Priya: On the harness adapter, will you support our custom retry policy? We use exponential backoff but with a max of 750ms for interactive flows.
[10:18] Diego: Yes, the adapter config allows retry policy overrides per route. For interactive we recommend keeping the max retry latency small to avoid poor user experience.
[10:28] Maya: Any blockers from your side to start the baseline?
[10:31] Priya: We just need the adapter example, and we need Redwood to accept our traffic dump. Also internal approval for sending a sample of PII redacted logs to Redwood for the run.
[10:42] Maya: We'll accept a redacted sample. We'll also provide an NDA addendum if needed.
[10:47] Liam: One more detail — our embeddings pipeline expects deterministic batching semantics: given input batch order, output must align. Will batching reorder?
[10:55] Diego: No reordering by default; the runtime keeps output ordering per batch id. If you use parallel batch shards, we'll reassemble preserving order. We'll document the guarantee.
[11:06] [11:30] Priya: For the quality eval, we will use semantic-similarity via our in-house metric. Can Redwood compute and return similarity scores as part of the report?
[11:37] Nina: Yes, we can compute similarity as part of the post-processing step if you provide the golden set.
[11:44] Jordan: Okay, timeline recap?
[11:47] Maya: We propose: Day 0-2: exchange artifacts (scripts, trace, security checklist). Day 3-5: Redwood sets up sandbox and runs a smoke test. Day 6-8: 48h baseline. Day 10: 4h stress window and final report by Day 12.
[12:07] Priya: That timeline is fine. We'll need a calendar invite for the baseline start.
[12:11] Maya: I'll put tentative invites.
[12:14] Diego: Anything else on tooling? We also support a lightweight CLI harness that can run your Go scripts to generate load; saves you wiring the streaming client yourself.
[12:23] Liam: That could speed things up. We'll try the CLI first.
[12:27] Priya: Ok, next steps recap?
[12:30] Maya: Action items: I'll share the adapter link and sample report. Diego will produce the streaming vs batch perf matrix. Priya will send traffic trace and tokenization sample. Jordan will send security checklist and network diagram.
[12:44] Priya: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[12:47] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up via email with links.
[12:50] [13:00] End of recording.

Notes on transcription: occasional misattribution (Speaker 6), filler words removed in places, some technical terms may be slightly garbled (K-V cash -> KV cache).
